pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Variation in Species

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Science, biology — 'the variation between individuals within a species being continuous or discontinuous, to include measurement and graphical representation of variation' and 'differences between species'):** This is the explicit KS3 statement, with an embedded working-scientifically requirement to MEASURE variation and REPRESENT it graphically — the graphing is part of the objective, not an add-on.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS3-2 and MS-LS4-4):** MS-LS3-2 — '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS3-1, MS-LS3-2].' MS-LS4-4 draws on variation as the raw material selection acts on. The 'why sexual reproduction produces more variation' evidence point maps directly onto MS-LS3-2.

- **Operational details:** Variation is the differences between living things — within a species (two humans) and between species. Two crosscutting distinctions must be built. (1) Continuous vs discontinuous: continuous variation takes any value across a range and, plotted, gives a smooth spread/bell (height, hand span, mass); discontinuous variation falls into distinct separate categories with nothing between (blood group, tongue-rolling, earlobe type) and plots as separate bars. The reliable diagnostic: can you have an in-between value? Height yes (continuous), blood group no (discontinuous). (2) Genetic vs environmental cause: some variation is inherited (eye colour, blood group), some is caused by environment (a scar, a suntan, language spoken, a plant stunted by poor soil), and many traits are BOTH (height = genes set a potential, nutrition determines how much is realised). The teaching move is hands-on: measure a real trait across the class, plot it, and read the graph shape to classify the variation — then reason about causes. Tie the greater variation from sexual reproduction back to the reproduction record: mixing two parents' alleles shuffles the deck.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (relational to early quantitative, lower secondary). Pupils measure, graph and classify, and reason about causes. Mastery = classifies a trait as continuous or discontinuous (with the in-between test), interprets/draws the matching graph, attributes variation to genetic, environmental or both, and explains why sexual reproduction generates more variation.
bestPractices: Make it hands-on and data-driven: have pupils MEASURE a real trait across the class (height, hand span) and a categorical one (blood group, tongue-rolling), then plot both — the curriculum names measurement and graphing as part of the objective.

Teach the graph SHAPE as the diagnostic: continuous variation gives a smooth spread/bell over a range; discontinuous gives separate bars with gaps — pupils should read 'shape of distribution' back to 'type of variation'.
Give pupils the reliable test for the continuous/discontinuous split — 'can there be an in-between value?' — which resolves most borderline cases better than memorising examples.
Handle genetic vs environmental as often-BOTH, using height (genes set potential, nutrition realises it) as the anchor, so pupils don't force every trait into one bin.
Link greater variation under sexual reproduction back to the reproduction/inheritance work — two parents' alleles are shuffled — rather than presenting it as an isolated fact (MS-LS3-2).
keyRepresentations: A histogram/frequency curve of a measured continuous trait (class heights) showing a smooth bell over a range.
A bar chart of a discontinuous trait (blood groups, tongue-rolling) showing separate categories with gaps.
A side-by-side of the two graph shapes as the visual signature of continuous vs discontinuous.
A cause table sorting traits into genetic / environmental / both, with height flagged as 'both'; plus a simple allele-shuffling diagram showing sexual reproduction combining two parents' variation.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing continuous and discontinuous — e.g. treating shoe size (really discontinuous/categorical due to sizing) or eye colour as continuous, without applying the 'in-between value?' test.
Thinking a trait must be EITHER genetic OR environmental, missing that many (height, mass) are both.
Believing all variation is inherited/genetic, overlooking environmental variation (scars, tan, learned language, diet effects).
Assuming environmentally-caused (acquired) variation can be passed to offspring — a Lamarckian slip that must be pre-empted before natural selection is taught.
Reading a bell-shaped graph as 'discontinuous' or a bar chart as 'continuous' — not connecting graph shape to variation type.
Thinking asexual and sexual reproduction produce similar variation, missing that asexual gives clones (identical) while sexual shuffles alleles.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–13 learn variation within and between species by measuring real traits, plotting them, and reading the graph shape to classify variation as continuous or discontinuous, then reasoning about whether differences are genetic, environmental or both, and why sexual reproduction generates more variation than asexual reproduction. The central working-scientifically skill — measure, plot, classify — is named by the curriculum and should be experienced through data collection, not only recognised. Alternatives (classification/interpretation practice, a reference gallery, and a Socratic dialogue) are retained for their distinct pedagogical purposes.

activities.title: Variation lab: measure, plot, classify
feedback: If a learner reads a bell-shaped graph as 'discontinuous' or a bar chart as 'continuous', point them back to the in-between test: ask whether a value between two recorded points is possible for that trait.
If a learner classifies height as coming in 'types' (tall/medium/short), have them measure several more people and watch intermediate values fill the gaps.
When the nutrition slider moves the height curve but not the blood-group bars, prompt: which trait did the environment change, and which stayed fixed — and what does that tell you about their causes?
When comparing clone vs two-parent offspring, ask the learner to explain where the spread came from (mixing two parents' alleles).
activities.rationale: The standard explicitly includes measurement and graphical representation of variation, so building the classification through live data collection targets the named skill rather than teaching the result as a fact. Reading graph shape back to variation type and using the in-between test address the most common classification errors.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 biology requires 'the variation between individuals within a species being continuous or discontinuous, to include measurement and graphical representation of variation' and study of differences between species.

Continuous variation (any value across a range, e.g. height) plots as a smooth/normal distribution; discontinuous variation (distinct categories, e.g. blood group) plots as separate bars — standard biology treatment.
learnerActions: Choose a continuous trait (e.g. height or hand span) and record it person-by-person across the class (or a virtual population), adding each value to a building histogram/frequency graph.

Watch the values spread across a continuous range with no natural gaps as more data arrive; with a large sample this often approaches a smooth, roughly bell-shaped curve, though a single class's histogram may be lumpy or uneven.

Switch to a categorical trait such as blood group (A/B/AB/O) and record again, watching the graph stack into separate bars with no values between them. (Tongue-rolling or earlobe type are often used too, but real earlobes show intermediate forms and tongue-rolling is not purely genetic, so blood group is the clearest example.)

Compare the two graph shapes side by side and state the rule in your own words: 'if there can be an in-between value, it's continuous; if it falls into distinct separate categories, it's discontinuous'.
Apply the 'can there be an in-between value?' test to borderline cases (e.g. shoe size, eye colour) and justify your classification.

If available, drag a 'nutrition/environment' slider and observe the modelled height distribution shift (for example, better nutrition moving it towards greater heights) while the blood-group bars do not move; describe what this shows about genetic vs environmental influence.

If available, use a reproduction toggle in an idealised model that holds the environment constant to compare clones from asexual reproduction (genetically identical offspring, shown as a single bar) with offspring of two parents (a spread, because sexual reproduction mixes alleles from both parents). Note that real clones can still differ because of their environment.
activities.intendedInsight: The shape of a distribution is the visible signature of the type of variation: continuous traits spread across a range with no gaps (approaching a smooth curve with large samples), while discontinuous traits fall into discrete columns. Environment can shift a continuous distribution (height) while leaving a purely inherited categorical trait (blood group) unchanged, and sexual reproduction's mixing of alleles from two parents is the source of greater genetic variety among offspring.

activities.title: Predict-then-plot the class height graph
feedback: If the learner predicted distinct groups, don't just mark it wrong — ask what the actual plotted values between the 'groups' show.
Treat the reason given beforehand as the diagnostic: a prediction of discrete types signals a continuous/discontinuous confusion to address directly.
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain cycle surfaces the learner's prior model before the data arrive, so the contrast between expectation and the measured distribution does the teaching.
sourceClaims: Continuous variation (any value across a range, e.g. height) plots as a smooth/normal distribution; discontinuous variation (distinct categories, e.g. blood group) plots as separate bars — standard biology treatment.
learnerActions: Before any measuring, predict the shape of a graph of everyone's height: will people fall into a few distinct groups (short/medium/tall) or spread smoothly across a range?
Commit to your prediction in writing and state your REASON first.
Measure and plot the real class heights.

Compare the plotted heights with your prediction: look for values spread across a range with no natural gaps between 'groups' (a single class may give an uneven histogram rather than a perfect bell), and revise your reasoning if you expected distinct types.
activities.intendedInsight: Many learners expect height to come in discrete categories; confronting that prediction with real measured heights spread continuously across a range makes the continuous-variation idea stick and exposes the reasoning behind any misclassification.

activities.title: Sort traits by type and by cause
feedback: If a learner forces every trait into a single cause, revisit height: genes set a range, diet and health determine where in that range you land.

If a learner mislabels blood group (or tongue-rolling, recorded as can/cannot) as continuous, return to whether an in-between value exists; note that earlobe attachment is less clear-cut because intermediate forms occur.
Examples to reuse: genetic (eye colour, blood group); environmental (a scar, a suntan, language spoken, a plant stunted by poor soil); both (height, mass).
activities.rationale: Crisp categorisation and graph-interpretation tasks check these targets efficiently, but they assess classification after the fact rather than building it through measuring and plotting, so pair them with the data-collection activity rather than substituting for it.
learnerActions: Sort a set of trait cards into continuous vs discontinuous, applying the in-between test to justify each.
Sort the same or additional traits into genetic / environmental / both, placing height deliberately in 'both' (genes set a potential, nutrition determines how much is realised).
Match a given bell curve or bar chart to the correct variation type.
Read a supplied frequency graph (histogram) and state what it shows about the trait.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification has two independent axes — continuous/discontinuous (graph shape) and genetic/environmental/both (cause) — and traits like height occupy 'both' rather than one bin.

activities.title: Reference gallery: trait cards and graph signatures
feedback: Direct learners to the in-between flap whenever they hesitate on a classification.
Use the gallery as a pre-teach or quick reference, then move to real data collection for the working-scientifically skill.
activities.rationale: A tappable reference pre-teaches vocabulary and graph shapes well; its limit is that it cannot let pupils generate data and watch a distribution emerge, which is the core skill named by the standard.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 biology requires 'the variation between individuals within a species being continuous or discontinuous, to include measurement and graphical representation of variation' and study of differences between species.
learnerActions: Explore a gallery where each trait card reveals its type, its graph shape, and its cause(s).
Use a lift-the-flap 'can you have an in-between?' prompt on each card to rehearse the diagnostic test.
Study a side-by-side of the two graph signatures (smooth bell vs separate bars) as a reference before or alongside the lab.
Consult a cause table that sorts traits into genetic / environmental / both, with height flagged as 'both'.
activities.intendedInsight: A clean reference anchors the vocabulary and the two graph signatures and can carry the cause table, supporting recall of the continuous/discontinuous and genetic/environmental distinctions.

activities.title: Talk it through with a geneticist (dialogue)
feedback: If the learner says acquired traits (a tan, trained muscles) are inherited, anchor to DNA: training doesn't change the alleles in sperm or eggs, so the effect isn't heritable; only differences written in the DNA are passed on.
If the learner forces a both-causes trait into one bin, ask them to separate what the genes set from what the environment realises.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning can surface and challenge the either/or and Lamarckian misconceptions through justification; its limit is that talk leaves the distributions abstract, so it complements rather than replaces measuring and graphing.
learnerActions: Discuss with a geneticist persona whether a chosen trait (e.g. height) is genetic, environmental or both, and justify your classification.
Respond to the challenge 'is a suntan — or a weightlifter's trained muscles — passed on to your children?' and explain why or why not.
Explain why the children of the same two parents vary from one another rather than being identical.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending classifications surfaces the either/or misconception and the Lamarckian 'acquired traits are inherited' slip, which must be pre-empted before natural selection is taught.

constraints: The curriculum names measurement and graphical representation of variation as part of the objective, so pupils should actually collect data and build graphs, not only recognise finished charts.

Classification quizzes, the reference gallery and the dialogue rehearse or assess classification but do not themselves build the measure-plot-classify skill; use them alongside, not instead of, real data collection.
Pre-empt the Lamarckian misconception (acquired/environmentally-caused traits are NOT inherited) before teaching natural selection.
Treat traits like height as 'both' genetic and environmental; avoid forcing every trait into a single cause.
A slider that shifts a distribution and a reproduction toggle are illustrative interaction examples to make the mechanism concrete; they are optional, not mandatory, and model idealised data.
Virtual populations and live-rebuilding graphs are models; where possible, ground the work in real measured class data for the continuous trait.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (NGSS MS-LS3-2 and BBC Bitesize) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.

The geneticist dialogue's sourceClaims are [] because no cited source claim directly supports its teaching principle (Socratic surfacing of the either/or and Lamarckian misconceptions); the NGSS reproduction claim supports the topic, not the method.

The original row asserts a 3D environment 'adds nothing' over a 2D tool; this comparative-efficacy/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been omitted rather than propagated. A 2D data-and-graph representation is a reasonable fit for statistical/categorical content, but no universal 'only this teaches' claim is warranted.

Shoe size is cited in the misconceptions as discontinuous/categorical 'due to sizing'; this depends on the measurement scheme (underlying foot length is continuous). It is used only as a borderline case for the in-between test, not taught as a fixed fact.

Eye colour is treated as a discontinuous/categorical example at KS3 level; actual inheritance is polygenic, so it is used only as a classification example, not a biological definition. It appears as a 'genetic' cause example and as a borderline type case on separate axes (cause vs type), which is not a contradiction.

The diagnostic weightlifter scenario and its correct answer are preserved from the assess field and are consistent with the activities; the prerequisite reteach IDs referenced there are catalog internals and were not carried into learner-facing guidance.

'Earlobe type' was added to Activity 1 (and Activity 3 feedback) so that the discontinuous example named in the source and listed in the preservation audit is genuinely present in the learner content.

assess.poeTask: Before plotting, ask students to predict the shape of a graph of everyone's height in the class: will people fall into a few distinct groups (short/medium/tall) or spread smoothly across a range? Have them commit to a prediction and state their REASON first. Then measure and plot — the smooth bell-shaped spread of continuous variation confronts the common prediction of distinct categories. The diagnostic part is the reason given beforehand: whether they expect discrete types or a continuum.
probeDeeper: His children turn out taller than average too — is that from his training, or something else? How could you tell the difference?
Is height continuous or discontinuous variation? What would a graph of your whole class's heights look like?
Why do the children of the same two parents vary from each other, instead of being identical copies?
assess.correctAnswer: No. The big muscles are an acquired, environmental characteristic caused by training — not a change to his DNA — so they aren't passed on. His children inherit his genes (which might include some tendency for build), but not the results of his training. Only genetic variation is inherited; environmentally-caused variation is not.

errorPatterns.pattern: Inheritance of acquired characteristics — 'traits you build in your lifetime pass to your children'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor to DNA: training doesn't change the alleles in his sperm, so the effect isn't heritable; only differences written in the DNA are passed on.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — his years of training will be passed on, so his children will be born stronger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees the children will be born stronger because of the father's training

errorPatterns.pattern: A trait has only one cause — 'height is entirely down to your genes' (or entirely diet)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use height: genes set a range, diet and health determine where in that range you land — many traits are both.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes a both-causes trait (height, weight) wholly to genetics or wholly to environment

errorPatterns.pattern: Continuous/discontinuous confusion — 'height comes in types: tall, medium, short'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a smooth spread (height, measurable at any value) with distinct categories (blood group A/B/AB/O); plot each to see the different graph shapes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies a continuous trait as falling into distinct groups, or treats a discontinuous trait like blood group as a smooth range

responseLevels.gap: Says acquired traits are inherited (children born stronger); treats a trait as one-cause-only or muddles continuous with discontinuous.
responseLevels.full: Identifies the muscles as environmental (not in the DNA, so not inherited), distinguishes genetic from environmental causes for a both-causes trait, classifies continuous vs discontinuous correctly, explains sexual reproduction as the source of offspring variety, and transfers to a new trait.
responseLevels.partial: Says the muscles come from training and might not be inherited, but can't cleanly state that only genetic variation is heritable, or lists continuous/discontinuous examples without explaining the genetic-vs-environmental split or why sexual reproduction increases variation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A weightlifter has trained for years and has huge muscles. A student says his children will be born stronger than average because of all his training. Is that right? Explain using the idea of genetic and environmental causes of variation.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who separates genetic from environmental causes rejects the claim and labels the muscles environmental. A child holding the classic Lamarckian inheritance-of-acquired-traits idea agrees the children will be born stronger — opposite answers, and it's the best-documented variation error.
